attribution: All descriptions paraphrase Peter Dale Scott or sources he quotes. Interpretations and allegations are attributed; inclusion is not independent verification. PDF citations use exact 1-based file pages.

source.title: The State, the Deep State, and the Wall Street Overworld
source.author: Peter Dale Scott
source.dateNote: Header gives March 3, 2014; recommended citation on PDF p19 gives March 10, 2014. The article says updated March 13.

people.name: Peter Dale Scott
people.description: Author who argues that intelligence agencies, financial interests and intermediaries form a supranational deep political system.

people.name: Mike Lofgren
people.description: Scott quotes his distinction between public government and a less visible system, and his argument about Wall Street incentives.

people.name: Dana Priest
people.description: Co-author with William Arkin of Top Secret America, quoted in the introduction.

people.name: William Arkin
people.description: Co-author with Dana Priest of the account of expanding classified government cited by Scott.

people.name: Tom Hayden
people.description: Scott quotes his interpretation of the Obama administration and the 2009 Honduras coup.

people.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
people.description: Scott cites a 1933 statement to Edward House and discusses Roosevelt’s unconditional-surrender policy.

people.name: Nelson Aldrich
people.description: Scott names him among participants associated with the secret 1910 banking meeting.

people.name: Paul Warburg
people.description: Scott cites his later recollection of secrecy around the banking conference.

people.name: Hoyt Vandenberg
people.description: Scott says he recruited Allen Dulles in 1946 to advise on the future CIA.

people.name: Allen W. Dulles
people.description: Scott traces his Sullivan and Cromwell practice, CIA planning, European political operations, and support for the Iran operation.

people.name: William H. Jackson
people.description: Named by Scott as a member of Dulles’s advisory group who later joined the CIA.

people.name: Frank Wisner
people.description: Scott describes his move from Wall Street into the Office of Policy Coordination.

people.name: George Kennan
people.description: Scott cites his involvement with Dulles and Forrestal in the Marshall Plan’s covert funding provision.

people.name: James Forrestal
people.description: Scott associates him with planning the covert political warfare provision attached to reconstruction aid.

people.name: Irving Brown
people.description: Scott, citing Douglas Valentine, alleges involvement in drug smuggling alongside anti-communist labor organizing.

people.name: Jay Lovestone
people.description: Scott identifies him as a CIA asset and Brown’s superior.

people.name: Pierre Ferri-Pisani
people.description: Scott alleges that he used CIA-linked labor funds for violence against Communist dockworkers.

people.name: Yoshio Kodama
people.description: Scott describes him as a CIA asset and distributor of Lockheed payments; drug-related claims follow Scott’s cited sources.

people.name: Prince Bernhard
people.description: Scott names him as a Lockheed payment beneficiary, Dulles and Bedell Smith friend, and Bilderberg organizer.

people.name: Walter Bedell Smith
people.description: Named as a friend of Prince Bernhard in Scott’s discussion of Lockheed payments.

people.name: August Munir Dasaad
people.description: Scott describes his Lockheed agency and contacts through General Alamsjah.

people.name: General Alamsjah
people.description: Scott identifies him as beneficiary of a Lockheed account and financial supporter of Suharto.

people.name: Sukarno
people.description: Scott examines business payments and covert policy preceding his removal from power.

people.name: Suharto
people.description: Scott links his rise to military, shipping, oil and intermediary networks.

people.name: Bob Hasan
people.description: Scott describes him as aircraft commission agent and Suharto business partner.

people.name: Ibnu Sutowo
people.description: Scott identifies him as head of Permina and an ally of Suharto.

people.name: John Foster Dulles
people.description: Scott discusses his defense of cartels and links between Sullivan and Cromwell and foreign policy.

people.name: Karl Wolff
people.description: Scott discusses Dulles’s 1945 surrender negotiations with him and the dispute over Washington’s instructions.

people.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
people.description: Scott discusses oil antitrust policy, U-2 authorization and approval of TP/AJAX.

people.name: Harold Macmillan
people.description: Scott says a 1957 arrangement allowed British authorization of certain U-2 flights.

people.name: Arthur Dean
people.description: Scott quotes his refusal to surrender oil-cartel documents on national-security grounds.

people.name: Mohammad Mossadeq
people.description: Scott places oil nationalization, export restrictions and the coup within an oil-company-centered interpretation.

people.name: Harry S. Truman
people.description: Scott describes his antitrust investigation and refusal to support a CIA overthrow of Mossadeq.

people.name: Winston Churchill
people.description: Scott says his appeal for CIA intervention in Iran was declined by Truman.

people.name: Averell Harriman
people.description: Scott describes his unsuccessful negotiating mission to Tehran.

people.name: William Eddy
people.description: Scott identifies him as an undercover CIA-connected adviser to ARAMCO.

people.name: Mike McConnell
people.description: Scott uses his movement between NSA, DNI and Booz Allen to illustrate the revolving door.

people.name: Edward Snowden
people.role: Booz Allen employee and disclosure source
people.description: Scott connects press attention to Booz Allen with his departure carrying NSA records.

people.name: Edward Lansdale
people.description: Scott associates him with Philippine land redistribution and anti-Huk policy.

people.name: Miles Copeland, Jr.
people.description: Scott examines his Booz Allen work, Nasser advice, Khashoggi ties and private intelligence claims; notes that some writers find his memoirs unreliable.

people.name: Gamal Abdel Nasser
people.description: Scott describes Copeland’s advice to him on intelligence organization.

people.name: Adnan Khashoggi
people.description: Scott traces commissions, political contacts and Iran-Contra financing; some corruption stories are explicitly contested in the notes.

people.name: Larry Kolb
people.description: Scott uses his eyewitness account of the 1985 Hamburg meeting and records his rejection of the Nixon briefcase story.

people.name: Kamal Adham
people.description: Scott describes Khashoggi’s business partner, BCCI shareholder and a principal CIA contact.

people.name: Edward K. Moss
people.description: Scott identifies Khashoggi’s Washington agent, CIA political-action contact and Kenyan Safari Club chairman.

people.name: Richard Nixon
people.description: Scott discusses contacts with Khashoggi, Rebozo banking and alleged campaign money, with contradictory accounts in note 83.

people.name: Bebe Rebozo
people.description: Scott discusses Khashoggi accounts at his Florida bank and alleged Paradise Island transfers.

people.name: Howard Hughes
people.description: Scott connects his defense-contract and casino milieu to Khashoggi investments and travel.

people.name: Paul Helliwell
people.description: Scott describes his roles establishing Sea Supply and CAT and his association with Castle Bank.

people.name: E. P. Barry
people.description: Scott describes postwar counterintelligence and gold recovery, later banking partnerships.

people.name: Turki bin Faisal
people.description: Scott quotes his account of the 1976 Safari Club as compensation for US congressional intelligence restrictions.

people.name: Alexandre de Marenches
people.description: Scott presents the conventional account of him initiating the Safari Club, alongside Mamdani’s different account.

people.name: Henry Kissinger
people.description: Scott cites Mamdani’s claim that the Safari Club was formed with his blessing.

people.name: Richard Helms
people.description: Scott cites Trento on his alleged work with Safari Club networks beyond congressional review.

people.name: Theodore Shackley
people.role: CIA officer and private intelligence operator
people.description: Scott quotes Trento’s account of private intelligence arrangements and notes ownership of J. J. Cappucci and Associates.

people.name: James Angleton
people.description: Scott discusses his 1974 dismissal and quotes Trento’s account of his reaction.

people.name: William Colby
people.description: Scott discusses his dismissal of Angleton and criticism from other officers.

people.name: George H. W. Bush
people.description: Scott discusses Carlyle advice, post-CIA banking, and claims about BCCI financing attributed to Trento and Phillips.

people.name: Jimmy Carter
people.description: Scott discusses congressional reforms and restrained intelligence policies during his administration.

people.name: Anwar al-Sadat
people.description: Scott cites the Safari Club’s claimed facilitation of his 1977 Jerusalem visit.

people.name: Yitzhak Rabin
people.description: Scott cites Mamdani on his message to Sadat routed through a Moroccan representative.

people.name: Manucher Ghorbanifar
people.description: Scott compares memoir, Draper and congressional accounts of his work with Khashoggi in Iran-Contra.

people.name: Adolph (Al) Schwimmer
people.description: Scott identifies him among Hamburg meeting participants and earlier Khashoggi contacts.

people.name: David Kimche
people.description: Scott names him among Israelis associated with Khashoggi and a 1982 Kenya meeting.

people.name: Yaacov Nimrodi
people.description: Scott names him among participants in the 1982 Kenyan meeting.

people.name: Ariel Sharon
people.description: Scott identifies him at a 1982 meeting with Sudan’s president at the Kenyan resort.

people.name: Jaafar Nimeiri
people.description: Scott identifies him at the May 1982 Kenya meeting.

people.name: Robert McFarlane
people.description: Scott describes Copeland and Kolb papers prepared for him on Middle East peace and Iran.

people.name: Bruce Rappaport
people.description: Scott examines BCCI interlocks through his Swiss banking business and cites intelligence-link claims.

people.name: Alfred Hartmann
people.description: Scott describes overlapping positions at BCCI, its Swiss subsidiary and Rappaport’s bank.

people.name: Bandar bin Sultan
people.description: Scott cites reported al-Yamamah payments and Saudi Embassy banking.

people.name: Richard Kerr
people.description: Scott cites his Senate acknowledgment that CIA used BCCI for intelligence gathering.

organizations.name: Central Intelligence Agency
organizations.description: US intelligence agency central to Scott’s examination of covert operations and private-sector connections.

organizations.name: Federal Bureau of Investigation
organizations.description: Scott cites its communications about Moss and allegations that authorities did not act on BCCI warnings.

organizations.name: National Security Agency
organizations.description: US signals intelligence agency discussed through contractors and McConnell’s career.

organizations.name: Sullivan and Cromwell
organizations.description: Wall Street law firm used by Scott to examine ties among oil companies, legal work and foreign policy.

organizations.name: Council on Foreign Relations
organizations.description: Scott says Dulles discussed Guatemala policy in this New York foreign-policy organization.

organizations.name: Federal Reserve System
organizations.description: Scott connects its antecedents to the 1910 banking meeting and discusses its 2008 rescue role.

organizations.name: American Committee for a United Europe
organizations.description: Scott describes Dulles establishing it in 1948 to support European integration.

organizations.name: Office of Policy Coordination
organizations.description: Covert political operations office headed by Wisner in Scott’s account.

organizations.name: American Federation of Labor
organizations.description: Labor organization whose officials Scott discusses in anti-communist political operations.

organizations.name: Economic Cooperation Administration
organizations.description: Agency created in 1948 to administer Marshall Plan assistance.

organizations.name: Sea Supply Inc.
organizations.description: Scott describes a CIA-controlled supply firm supporting Southeast Asian forces and drug-linked armies.

organizations.name: CAT Inc. / Air America
organizations.description: Scott identifies the aviation company Helliwell helped establish for CIA operations.

organizations.name: Police Aerial Reinforcement Unit
organizations.description: CIA-supported Thai paramilitary force discussed with Sea Supply infrastructure.

organizations.name: Lockheed
organizations.description: Aerospace and defense contractor whose overseas payments Scott compares across countries.

organizations.name: Bilderberg Group
organizations.description: International gathering identified by Scott with Prince Bernhard as organizer.

organizations.name: Rockwell-Standard
organizations.description: Aircraft company associated with a July 1965 Indonesian Army delivery agreement.

organizations.name: Diponegoro Division
organizations.description: Indonesian Army division Scott connects to Suharto business interests and both sides of the 1965 coup drama.

organizations.name: Stanvac
organizations.description: Standard-company joint venture Scott says increased payments to Permina in 1965.

organizations.name: Permina
organizations.description: Indonesian army oil company led by Ibnu Sutowo.

organizations.name: Seven Sisters oil cartel
organizations.description: Collective oil-company label used in Scott’s argument about export control and Iran; not a formally incorporated institution.

organizations.name: Anglo-Iranian Oil Company / BP
organizations.description: British oil company at the center of Scott’s discussion of Iranian nationalization and the 1953 coup.

organizations.name: Arabian-American Oil Company (ARAMCO)
organizations.description: Saudi oil company discussed through production expansion and CIA-linked advisers.

organizations.name: Secret Intelligence Service (MI6)
organizations.description: British intelligence service discussed in Iran and U-2 flight arrangements.

organizations.name: Booz Allen Hamilton
organizations.description: Consultancy and intelligence contractor central to Scott’s revolving-door and overseas mission account.

organizations.name: Booz and Company
organizations.description: Commercial and international consulting successor created by the 2008 split.

organizations.name: Carlyle Group
organizations.description: Private equity owner of Booz Allen discussed through Bush family connections.

organizations.name: Egyptian Mukhabarat
organizations.description: Egyptian intelligence service Scott says Copeland advised Nasser on establishing.

organizations.name: Bank of Credit and Commerce International
organizations.description: Bank examined by Scott for political influence, intelligence financing and Iran-Contra loans.

organizations.name: Mount Kenya Safari Club
organizations.description: Kenyan resort associated with Moss and Khashoggi; distinct from the intelligence alliance using the same name.

organizations.name: Safari Club intelligence alliance
organizations.description: 1976 alliance of French, Egyptian, Saudi, Moroccan and Iranian services. Scott contrasts official-policy origins with alleged later circumvention of restrictions.

organizations.name: Service de Documentation Extérieure et de Contre-Espionnage
organizations.description: French intelligence service led by de Marenches.

organizations.name: Castle Bank and Trust
organizations.description: Helliwell-associated bank discussed through Operation Tradewinds and a Nixon-name account.

organizations.name: Paradise Island Bridge Company
organizations.description: Bahamas business discussed through alleged Nixon transfers and Booz Allen-linked ownership.

organizations.name: First International Bancshares
organizations.description: Banking group whose executive committee Bush chaired after leaving CIA, according to Phillips quoted by Scott.

organizations.name: Bank of New York-Intermaritime
organizations.description: Rappaport-associated Swiss banking institution linked by Scott to BCCI through shared executives.

organizations.name: Banque de Commerce et de Placements
organizations.description: BCCI Swiss subsidiary Scott describes as headed by Alfred Hartmann.

organizations.name: Bank of England
organizations.description: Scott cites a Senate report allegation that it withheld BCCI fraud information.

organizations.name: Riggs Bank
organizations.description: Washington bank used by the Saudi Embassy in Scott’s account of al-Yamamah payment channels.

organizations.name: J. J. Cappucci and Associates
organizations.description: Private US firm owned by Shackley that Scott’s notes link to Egyptian Army advisory work.

organizations.name: Office of Strategic Services
organizations.description: Wartime US intelligence service discussed through Dulles negotiations and Barry’s postwar gold recovery.

events.title: Secret banking conference at Jekyll Island
events.description: Scott connects a secret banking conference to the later Federal Reserve and cites Forbes and Warburg recollections; the meeting was an antecedent, not the legal creation of the System.

events.title: Roosevelt observation about financial power
events.description: Scott quotes Roosevelt’s statement to Edward House as an illustration of his interpretation of financial influence.

events.title: Dulles negotiates with Karl Wolff
events.description: Scott argues that Dulles’s negotiations over German forces in Italy evaded Washington instructions and undermined unconditional-surrender policy.

events.title: Dulles convenes CIA planning advisers
events.description: Scott says Vandenberg recruited Dulles, who assembled six advisers, mostly Wall Street lawyers or bankers, to plan the future CIA.

events.title: CIA-backed funding for Italian election
events.description: Scott cites captured Axis funds exceeding $10 million used to influence the Italian election; Dulles advocated public authorization of the operation.

events.title: American Committee for a United Europe established
events.description: Scott dates Dulles’s establishment of ACUE to early summer 1948 and links it to later CIA-backed European activity.

events.title: Marshall Plan funds support political warfare
events.description: Scott cites Weiner on a secret provision enabling CIA to divert reconstruction funds for covert political warfare.

events.title: Allen Dulles formally joins CIA
events.description: Scott contrasts Dulles’s formal entry in November 1950 with his earlier European activities.

events.title: Oil majors boycott Iranian exports
events.description: Scott argues that the oil majors supported AIOC’s export boycott; note 48 records Exxon’s corporate history denying a conspiracy to boycott NIOC oil.

events.title: Helliwell helps establish Sea Supply
events.description: Scott’s note 89 cites a 1980 Wall Street Journal account dating establishment of the CIA front to 1951.

events.title: Truman administration pursues oil-cartel case
events.description: Scott describes Justice Department efforts to break cartel agreements and Dean’s refusal to provide documents.

events.title: Royal Navy intercepts Iranian-oil tanker
events.description: Note 49 says the British Royal Navy diverted the Italian tanker Rose Mary to Aden, discouraging further attempts to reach Abadan.

events.title: CIA officials begin Iran-operation planning
events.description: Scott dates CIA planning to November 1952, distinguishing it from final presidential approval in July 1953.

events.title: Copeland returns to Cairo with Booz Allen mission
events.description: Scott quotes Copeland’s description of a joint CIA–Booz Allen mission and discusses advice to Nasser on intelligence organization.

events.title: Eisenhower approves TP/AJAX
events.description: Scott gives July 22 as the approval date and interprets the CIA operation as joining an earlier oil-company campaign.

events.title: Oil antitrust criminal case replaced by civil action
events.description: Scott argues that the incoming Eisenhower administration weakened the antitrust action against oil majors.

events.title: Booz Allen begins overseas assignments
events.description: Scott lists Philippine land registration, Egyptian economic work and Iranian oil-company work, arguing that each overlapped CIA activity.

events.title: British authorization channel arranged for U-2 flights
events.description: Scott, citing Dorril, says Dulles arranged for British authorization to bypass Eisenhower’s reluctance over additional flights.

events.title: CIA considers Moss for political action
events.description: Scott cites CIA documents about using Moss for the Covert Action staff’s Political Action Group; FBI allegations about associates are discussed separately.

events.title: CIA political action project against Indonesian PKI
events.description: Scott quotes a US decision to support obstructive action against the Indonesian Communist Party; note 37 gives the November 19 project date.

events.title: Lockheed shifts Indonesian intermediary contract
events.description: Scott says payments moved to Dasaad’s company over counsel objections and links the account to General Alamsjah.

events.title: Rockwell aircraft agreement with Indonesian Army
events.description: Scott describes an agreement for two hundred light aircraft and identifies Bob Hasan as commission agent.

events.title: Indonesian September coup drama
events.description: Scott notes that the Diponegoro division supplied personnel on both sides of the coup attempt and suppression; his causal network interpretation is not independently verified.

events.title: Copeland establishes close Khashoggi contact
events.description: Scott dates close contact to 1966 while Copeland was on leave from Booz Allen; Copeland’s retrospective private-CIA claims are qualified as controversial.

events.title: Khashoggi supplies plane for Nixon Middle East tour
events.description: Scott cites Summers on Khashoggi providing Nixon a plane after the Six-Day War and opening a Rebozo bank account through a proxy.

events.title: Lockheed commissions paid to Khashoggi
events.description: Scott cites Hartung on Lockheed’s acknowledgment of $106 million in Khashoggi commissions between 1970 and 1975.

events.title: Colby dismisses James Angleton
events.description: Scott quotes Trento interpreting Angleton’s dismissal as a stimulus for extramural intelligence cooperation.

events.title: Safari Club intelligence alliance established
events.description: Scott quotes Turki on its creation to compensate for US intelligence constraints, while also presenting Mamdani’s account of an authorized alliance with Kissinger’s blessing.

events.title: Bush takes post-CIA banking position
events.description: Scott quotes Phillips on Bush becoming executive-committee chair at First International Bancshares after leaving CIA.

events.title: Sadat visits Jerusalem
events.description: Scott cites Mamdani’s account that a message relayed through the Safari Club helped prepare Sadat’s visit.

events.title: Israeli and Sudanese figures meet at Kenyan resort
events.description: Scott cites Draper on Khashoggi’s resort hosting Nimeiri, Sharon, Nimrodi, Schwimmer and Kimche.

events.title: Khashoggi submits Middle East Peace Fund proposal
events.description: Scott’s note 73 cites Kessler on a confidential yellow paper to Reagan proposing regional aid; Scott associates Copeland and Kolb with its development.

events.title: Hamburg meeting prepares Iran arms initiative
events.description: Scott compares Draper, Copeland and Kolb accounts of Khashoggi and Ghorbanifar discussions. Copeland and Kolb describe broader strategic aims; congressional sources also identify arms financing.

events.title: BCCI collapses amid investigations
events.description: Scott discusses the summer 1991 collapse and congressional accounts of agency inaction on earlier warnings.

events.title: Kerry–Brown BCCI report published
events.description: Scott’s notes cite the Senate Foreign Relations report as the source for BCCI intelligence and Iran-Contra financing information.

events.title: Booz consulting firm splits
events.description: Scott describes separation of government-focused Booz Allen Hamilton from commercial and international Booz and Company.

events.title: Federal Reserve supports bank rescue
events.description: Scott interprets support across successive administrations for rescue of Wall Street banks as evidence of financial influence.

relationships.label: Recruited as planning adviser
relationships.description: Scott says Vandenberg recruited Dulles in 1946 to advise on the agency’s organization.

relationships.label: Advisory group colleague
relationships.description: Scott connects the two through CIA planning and later covert operations.

relationships.label: Brothers and policy colleagues
relationships.description: Scott analyzes their law-firm and government roles together.

relationships.label: Assistant to
relationships.description: Scott describes Brown as assistant to AFL official Lovestone.

relationships.label: Anti-communist labor funding
relationships.description: Scott alleges Brown and CIA funding supported Ferri-Pisani’s labor operations in Marseille.

relationships.label: Payment intermediary
relationships.description: Scott describes Kodama receiving and distributing Lockheed funds for procurement influence.

relationships.label: Payment beneficiary
relationships.description: Scott identifies Bernhard as beneficiary of Lockheed payments.

relationships.label: Indonesian agent
relationships.description: Scott identifies Dasaad as the firm’s longtime Indonesian intermediary.

relationships.label: Family connection
relationships.description: Scott says Dasaad connected to Suharto through relative General Alamsjah.

relationships.label: Financial support
relationships.description: Scott says Alamsjah supplied funds after Suharto replaced Sukarno.

relationships.label: Business partners
relationships.description: Scott describes their shipping companies operated with the Diponegoro division.

relationships.label: Increased oil payments
relationships.description: Scott connects increased Stanvac payments to Permina with Indonesia’s political transition.

relationships.label: Political ally
relationships.description: Scott describes Sutowo as an eventual Suharto ally.

relationships.label: Export boycott support
relationships.description: Scott argues the majors backed AIOC’s boycott; note 48 records a contrary Exxon corporate account.

relationships.label: Joint Iran operation
relationships.description: Scott discusses cooperation in TP/AJAX.

relationships.label: Majority owner in article
relationships.description: Scott describes majority ownership at the time of the article; this is historical, not a current ownership statement.

relationships.label: Intelligence adviser
relationships.description: Scott describes Copeland advising Nasser and acting as an important US-government channel.

relationships.label: Political and business collaborators
relationships.description: Scott describes close collaboration and Copeland’s private-intelligence claims, noting reliability concerns.

relationships.label: Assistant and collaborator
relationships.description: Scott uses Kolb’s account of work with Copeland on Khashoggi proposals.

relationships.label: Commission agent
relationships.description: Scott cites acknowledged commissions paid between 1970 and 1975.

relationships.label: Friends and business partners
relationships.description: Scott describes their friendship and business ties.

relationships.label: Washington public relations agent
relationships.description: Scott identifies Moss as Khashoggi’s public relations representative.

relationships.label: Cultivated political access
relationships.description: Scott discusses aircraft and banking assistance; note 83 disputes the sensational briefcase donation account.

relationships.label: Banking relationship

evidenceIssues.description: Publication header and recommended citation disagree (March 3 versus March 10); explicit update March 13, 2014.
Scott notes establishment writers describe Copeland memoirs as unreliable; claims from Copeland remain attributed.
Nixon briefcase donation story is disputed by Kolb, and Baer gives 1968 rather than 1972; not included as a factual dated event.
Safari Club resort and intelligence alliance are separate entities; Scott presents both official-policy origin and later circumvention interpretations.
Notes 103 and 105 explicitly state no published evidence Copeland was involved in Safari Club covert operations; no membership edge created.
Scott’s oil-boycott interpretation is denied by Exxon corporate history in note 48.
The article’s parenthetical company labels conflate Standard Oil of New York/Socony and California. A collective oil-cartel record avoids reproducing the naming error.
Ownership and job descriptions are historical statements as of the 2014 article, not claims about current roles.
